utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Mr. Registrar, could you have the accused brought in, please? (Accused brought in)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone is all set, everyone can hear me? The accused can hear me as well? Can you hear me, General Blaskic as well? Fine. So we are here for the first part of this morning's work. This is an open session, relative to two motions, one of them filed on 17th November by the Defence. This is for reconsideration of the decisions taken by the Chamber on the matter of admissibility of authentic exculpatory evidence. There have been several documents relating to that -- that was rather on 5th November there, the Prosecution's response, then 30th September. So there was a matter of admissibility there of the hearsay testimony, and that also gave rise to several documents, the latest one being quite recent. Mr. Registrar, my translation does not have a date on it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I apologise, the first date was September rather than November.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: At all events, this latest one seems very recent indeed. There has been a third motion issued very recently, this is from the Prosecutor, this motion seeks clarification of an order in which we required advanced disclosure of the names of witnesses, this was in advance of witnesses appearing in the trial. I do not know if it is a matter of language, of translation or whether it is a substantive matter, but at all events we will not be addressing that now, as we said the other day, because we do not have any reply on the part of the Defence. I am sure that will be forthcoming soon, and in December I am sure we will have occasion to address that. If there are no preliminary comments, I would suggest we move right on, that we ask Mr. Hayman to indicate briefly what he has to say with regard to the motion of 17th September, and then the other documents that the Defence have submitted and, of course, after that we will hear the Prosecution. So it is Mr. Hayman, is it? Please proceed, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, your Honours, learned counsel. Did your Honour indicate that you wished to begin with the hearsay motion or the motion re authentication?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No, I just took things in chronological order. I thought the first motion dated from 17th September, so that is one way of tackling the issue, but if you prefer beginning with hearsay, we could do that as well, but I thought it would be the motion for reconsideration of the ruling for exculpatory documentary evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If I could begin with the hearsay matter, your Honour, there is maybe a certain logical order to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: If you are introducing a point of logic, let me consult fellow judges. No problem with us beginning with the hearsay matter, so let us follow logic. If there is no objection on the part of the Prosecution? Fine Mr. Hayman, you have chosen the arm, so please go right ahead. We will begin with hearsay then.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would like to ask three questions and then briefly try and answer them with respect to this motion. The first question, it seems to the Defence, is: is there a limit on the use and method of presentation of hearsay or derivative evidence before this Tribunal? Second: what sources of authority might the Tribunal look to to answer that question? Third: what specific rule or rules does the Defence urge this Trial Chamber to adopt with respect to the use and method of presentation for hearsay or derivative evidence? With respect to the first question, "is there a limit on the use and method of presentation of hearsay evidence before this Tribunal", the Prosecutor's position, I think, fairly can be summarised that they maintain all questions relating to hearsay and derivative evidence go to weight and neither admissibility nor the form of presentation; that is hearsay evidence should simply come in, the way all other evidence comes in, and the Trial Chamber will sort it out and give each item of evidence the appropriate weight. While we the Defence do not doubt the great skills and talents of this Trial Chamber in sorting evidence and assigning weight, we suggest there are limits to the method of presentation of hearsay, because no one, including your learned honours, can sort and evaluate evidence without the proper identifying information concerning that evidence and the circumstances which gave rise to that evidence. We also maintain there must be a limit on the substantive use of hearsay because, among other things, of the constraints contained in Article 21(4)(e), which assures the accused the right to cross-examine all witnesses against him. No Trial Chamber, with all due respect to Trial Chamber II, which has issued a written ruling some time ago in the matter of hearsay, still no Trial Chamber has clearly articulated, we believe, what the limits on the use and method of presentation of hearsay are before this Tribunal. What Trial Chamber II has said is that a Trial Chamber should look at a hearsay statement, and the content of the statement and the circumstances in which it was made in order to determine sufficient reliability to make the statement probative evidence which is necessary for the Tribunal to admit it under Rule 89(C), which states that a Trial Chamber may admit evidence found to have probative value. The corollary, of course, is evidence without probative value should be excluded because we are all wasting our time admitting and studying and evaluating evidence that is not probative. We are not suggesting either a common law nor a civil law approach to hearsay. We believe that the specific procedures and practices before the Tribunal must be looked to in order to find what regulation of the use of hearsay is appropriate before this court. Question two: to what authorities or sources should this Tribunal look for guidance? There are certainly existing bodies of national and international law. Common law hearsay rules are well known, but I will not dwell on them. I simply note that at least in my jurisdiction, the United States, all hearsay rules apply equally with respect to jury proceedings and court proceedings or proceedings tried before professional judges. There is no distinction between the hearsay rules in my system between those two types of proceedings. The civil law approach is more interesting for me as a common law lawyer, certainly stimulating, and a dangerous topic for me to speak of given the company in this courtroom, but I will try. First, the law of the former Yugoslavia is of some importance, I think, and under the 1976 Yugoslav law on criminal procedure, in section 2.32(2), a witness is required to state the source of his or her evidence, they are required to identify if the testimony they are giving, in whole or in part, is based on derivative or hearsay testimony, and if it is derivative or hearsay in nature, the testimony to be sure is admissible, but it is generally suspect within the Yugoslav -- former Yugoslav law on criminal procedure. More vigorous limits on the use of hearsay appear in the European Human Rights Convention in section 6(3)(D), which assures the accused the right to examine witnesses against him. In this regard I note that this section of the Convention is indeed very similar to Article 21(4)(e) of the Tribunal Statute. So there is guidance, but it is not clear. There is room for interpretation and the Defence believes that this Trial Chamber and this Tribunal indeed should be a model for future international criminal law jurisprudence in this area. Where else can the Tribunal look? We submit that we should all look to sound fact-finding procedures in light of the unique procedures used by this Tribunal. The Prosecution urges that the first rule, if you will, if you can call it a rule, would be that a witness need not state with clarity whether their evidence is direct, that is percipient, or whether it is derivative, that is based on either oral hearsay or documents. To date, no rule has been enforced in this courtroom requiring what we would call a foundation to be laid, where evidence is derivative; that is the witnesses state that the testimony they are giving is derivative and how they came about that evidence. Indeed, we have seen in the Prosecutor's presentation that directs and derivative evidence have been totally intermixed with virtually no effort to distinguish. I can recall for the court the testimony of Abdulah Ahmic, not controversial testimony, I think, that is not my point, I am not challenging the substantive testimony, but we will recall, if the court will, the 24 or 29 homes in the area of Ahmici where Mr. Ahmic identified the victims by name and said they were all killed on the 16th or whatever of April 1993. On his direct examination, there was no foundation laid for that testimony. In the cross-examination of my colleague and co-counsel, it was revealed that Mr. Ahmic gained that information not from being on the scene, as you will recall he was hiding in a canal or a stream at the time, but from reading a newspaper after he arrived in Zenica. There are a number of comments one could make about that, but the basic comment is this court can read newspaper articles as well as anyone else, better, I would submit, and it is a more efficient and appropriate way for the court to obtain that type of information. But in any event, we think that a foundation should be laid and that the record should be clear as to where evidence is coming from and that the burden for that, and I will get to this in a moment, lies on the party putting that evidence forward. It is not sufficient to simply say, "it is a matter for cross-examination". Why, though, is, in terms of the integrity of the fact-finding processes of this Tribunal, why should hearsay or derivative evidence be treated any differently in terms of process? Well, several things come to mind. One is the statements of the declarant, the person making the out of court statement, were not made under oath. The oath is an important feature of any court proceedings, and here out of court statements are not under oath. They are frequently casual statements, they may be statements made in a humorous light, they may be statements made under duress; whatever they are, they are not under oath. Second, out of court statements by a declarant are made outside of the presence of your Honours, and you are denied the opportunity to observe the demeanour of the declarant. Third, the court is denied the opportunity to examine the declarant and put any clarifying questions that it may have to the declarant. Lastly fourth, and here I allude to the European Human Rights Convention, as well as Article 21 of this Tribunal's own Statute, where out of court statements are admitted, the accused through his counsel is denied the opportunity to cross-examine the declarant -- keeping in mind, of course, that the witness, if the witness is repeating out of court statements of another, the witness is not a witness to the matters being related, but simply a messenger, because the witness, the person who saw or heard and related verbally the contents of what he or she saw or heard is not here, they are somewhere else. They are not here to be examined, challenged, questioned, observed as to matters such as possible bias, ability to perceive the event or even possible fabrication. One reaches an extreme with respect to these problems where the out of court declarant is not even identified in the narrative being given by the witness, which we have named so-called "anonymous hearsay". In that circumstance, where the declarant is not even identified, the accused, through his counsel, we cannot investigate this speaker, this declarant. We cannot even attempt coherently to impeach the statements of the out of court declarant through other evidence or testimony because we do not know the identity of that declarant. Which brings me to my third and last question on this matter: what rule or rules in concrete terms does the Defence urge this Trial Chamber to consider and, if it finds it appropriate, adopt? First, we feel strongly there should be a rule of procedure governing the presentation of hearsay or derivative evidence. The court and the parties must be informed when hearsay evidence is given. It should not be mixed, inadvertently concealed or hidden in and among other evidence. A foundation needs to be laid for it, and it is not sufficient to leave the "clarification" of whether evidence is direct or hearsay to cross-examination. Number one, I think that procedure is not fair to the party conducting the cross-examination, whether it is the accused or the Prosecutor, and also as we have seen the need on the part of the cross-examining party to go through a witness's narrative and determine what is direct and what is based on hearsay, and chase down all the threads, it takes an incredibly long period of time to do so, it is redundant, it is wasteful and it need not be engaged in if there is a basic rule that a foundation should be laid for hearsay testimony. In this regard, what do the court and the parties need to know at the time hearsay evidence is admitted or considered? One, is the evidence hearsay? Is it direct or is it derivative? Two, if it is hearsay, who is the ultimate declarant? That is, who is the out of court speaker, and if it is double or triple hearsay, who are the intermediate declarants or messengers that were involved in the chain of statements which the witness in court is recounting. Third, what is the content of the statement? That is, a clear statement of, "I was told X", not something more general, but a clear statement of the content of the out of court statement, so that it is not confused and mixed with the witness's own opinions and observations. Fourth, we submit the court and the parties need to know, to the extent it is known by the witness, when and under what circumstances was the statement given. Ideally, this will include some time and place and even who else was present, but that may not be known in all circumstances, and we are not suggesting a dogmatic or doctrinaire rule in this regard, it should be a flexible and practical rule. What we are urging in terms of rule of process is a good trial practice in any system. It goes to establishing a foundation for a witness's testimony and it will contribute to the integrity of the fact-finding process before this Tribunal. If the Trial Chamber were inclined to adopt this kind of rule, how might it be implemented? Of course, that is a matter up to your Honours, but we modestly propose that one method would be when a witness is giving their initial narrative, they be told, "please tell us what you saw with your own eyes, what you experienced, and if you are relating something that you heard from another person, tell us that that was the case, so we will know". Then the burden should be placed on the parties, when they follow up on any derivative or hearsay testimony, to lay a more specific foundation, for example, "madam, did you have a conversation? When was it? What were you told?". Not lengthy questions, not time consuming, but they will contribute to the clarity of the fact-finding process in this case and indeed other cases if adopted in other matters. If adopted, this kind of a procedural rule would enable the court to identify any hearsay that it believes lacks sufficient indicia of reliability to be admitted. Even if the court declines to have any threshold requirement for admissibility, this type of a procedure would enable the court to have the facts, the tools that it needs to give a proper weight to hearsay evidence in your deliberations, which is critical to our client and our client's interests. Without that identifying information, how can any tryer of fact give proper weight to derivative evidence? It will serve to focus, if adopted, the witness's testimony on direct examination on the matters that they were percipient to and we believe would result in more efficient direct examinations, and it will clearly shorten cross-examination because the unfair burden on the cross-examining party of revisiting all the facts narrated and trying to sort out what was direct and what was derivative will be, if not totally lifted, certainly ameliorated. There is though a second rule we urge this Tribunal to consider, and that is not a rule of procedure, but a rule of substance. That would be a substantive rule that recognises to give meaningful effect to Article 21(4)(e) and Rule 89(C). There will be occasions when this court should exclude material hearsay statements whose admission would violate either one or both of these rules and what I mean is under Rule 89(C), if a statement does not have sufficient reliability to be probative it should be excluded and under Article 21, if admission of hearsay testimony would violate the accused's right to cross-examine the witness, the source, if you will (although that is not a word that has specific meaning, as we will see later this morning), that the court should have the power, we should recognise the power of the court to exclude hearsay statements under either or both of those rules, and I submit the court has already recognised the validity of exclusion of hearsay statements under Article 21 when it excluded the letter from President Izetbegovic that was proffered by the Prosecution in the very first days of this case. I submit that letter was excluded not because it lacked reliability under Rule 89(C), we had no reason to doubt it was not a letter from President Izetbegovic, but it was excluded under Article 21, because to deny the accused any ability to cross-examine the declarant, the author of that letter, would have been wrong. So we urge the court to recognise that both of these grounds can be, in appropriate circumstances, when found in the court's exercise of its discretion, legitimate grounds for excluding certain hearsay evidence. We are not seeking that the court scrutinise or catalogue hypothetical situations at all, we simply think that recognition of these two rules, one procedural and one substantive, will facilitate addressing this issue in the days and months ahead. Mr. President, your Honours, those are my comments with respect to the hearsay matter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hayman. Well, maybe you could add some points of clarification after we have heard the arguments from the Office of the Prosecution. Mr. Harmon, I assume?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, good morning, Mr. President, good morning, counsel. During the course of this trial, the Defence has initially urged the Trial Chamber to prohibit the admission of hearsay evidence and the Trial Chamber rejected this position. In its present motion, the Defence makes a standing objection to the admission of hearsay evidence without two requirements, the first being a foundation for such hearsay and the second being a judicial finding, I repeat a judicial finding of the trustworthiness of the out of court statement in question. The Defence further contends that there can be no evaluation of trustworthiness of hearsay statements unless a number of conditions are met. The first is that the court declarant, the out of court declarant is identified, and the time, the place, the circumstances and the content of the statement are specified by the witness. The Defence cites in its papers as an example of the type of hearsay evidence it seeks to exclude the testimony of Dr Fuad Zeco, who testified that while he was detained at the veterinary station and at the Dubravica school that multiple unidentified detainees identified the locations where they were forced by the HVO to dig trenches. The Defence seeks to impose conditions akin to those in a common law system on the Trial Chamber's ability to receive hearsay evidence and to evaluate hearsay evidence. Neither the Rules of the Tribunal nor the decision in the Tadic case required the conditions that the Defence now seeks to impose on the Trial Chamber. This Trial Chamber is an unique institution, it has its own rules. The uniqueness of the institution and the rules have been repeatedly acknowledged and are in fact acknowledged in the rules themselves, where they say the Chambers are not bound by national rules of evidence and any efforts by the Defence to impose upon the Chamber common law rules and procedures should be rejected. The rule of evidence that is applicable to the reception of evidence by the Trial Chamber is Rule 89, and the relevant subpart of that Rule is 89(C), which states: "A Chamber may admit any relevant evidence that it deems to have probative value." The two requirements in 89(C) that are set forth are (i) that the evidence be relevant and (ii) that it have probative value. The rule does not expressly require any specific type of foundation to be laid, nor does it require a judicial finding of trustworthiness for any particular type of evidence that it hears and receives. The Tadic decision, Mr. President and your Honours, was an unanimous decision and it recognised that reliability was a component of whether a piece of evidence had probative value. The decision also said that the Trial Chamber should pay attention to indicia of reliability, such as whether a statement is voluntary, truthful and trustworthy. The Trial Chamber in the Tadic decision suggested that the judges who are hearing hearsay evidence should consider the circumstances under which the evidence arose and the content of the statement, and we fully agree with the decision in this respect. In this case, Mr. President and your Honours, all of the judges in this chamber and in other chambers of the Tribunal are judges who are able to determine as a result of their experience and their training whether evidence is reliability and are able to determine what weight should be given to the particular piece of evidence. In making its determination of whether certain hearsay is reliable, the court may consider, among other factors, but not be bound by any particular factor, the demeanour and truthfulness of a witness, the extent to which a witness has any biases, the extent to which the testimony, the hearsay testimony that the witness is relating has been corroborated in part or in whole by other witnesses, the totality of the evidence in the course of the trial. For example, Mr. President and your Honours, a piece of hearsay evidence standing alone may appear to be of dubious reliability, but when assessed in context of all of the other evidence heard in the course of the trial, it may in the minds of the tryers of fact be assessed to be reliable in the final analysis. The contrary is also true. A piece of hearsay evidence that appears initially to be reliable at the outset may after listening to the totality of the evidence become quite obviously unreliable, or appear to be unreliable. In that regard, Mr. President, Rule 89(D) is critical to the issue raised by the Defence in this case. 89(D) states: "A Trial Chamber may exclude evidence if its probative value is substantially outweighed by the need to ensure a fair trial." Paragraph 19 of the Tadic opinion on hearsay states, and I quote: "Moreover, Sub-rule 89(D) provides further protection against the prejudice to the Defence for evidence that has been admitted as relevant and having probative value it may later be excluded. Pursuant to this Sub-rule, the trial judges have the opportunity to consider the evidence, place it in the context of the trial and then exclude it if it is substantially outweighed by the need to ensure a fair trial." Turning to the example cited by the Defence, the testimony of Dr Fuad Zeco about being informed by unidentified civilians that they were being forced to dig trenches at numerous locations, it was clearly hearsay. It has been received by this Trial Chamber. Should it be excluded? The Prosecutor would respectfully submit that it should not, for the following reasons. The Trial Chamber heard from Dr Zeco, a gentleman who was the local veterinarian in Vitez, it had an opportunity to observe him, to assess his demeanour and any possible biases he could have when he identified nine locations where civilians were taken by the HVO to dig trenches. The Trial Chamber also heard from Dr Zeco that during his period of captivity in both the veterinary station and in the Dubravica school, he had an unique opportunity to hear from fellow captives who had been taken to dig trenches. While in captivity, Mr. President, he testified that it became clear to him that many of the Muslim men who were being taken to dig trenches were being repeatedly taken out to dig trenches and they were bordering on, and in many cases were exhausted and as a result of that, he and two other men went to the commander of the Dubravica school, the HVO commander, and suggested a procedure whereby the Muslims themselves would select and identify the men who were needed to be taken out to dig trenches. That would essentially spread the pain more equally. You have heard, Mr. President, from other witnesses -- from another witness that the Croat commander came into the Dubravica school and at one point requested that the Muslims identify men who were needed to dig trenches. That corroborated what Dr Zeco had to say. The Chamber has also heard from various civilians themselves who were taken to various different locations to dig trenches, and the court has heard that civilians were taken on a daily basis by the HVO from the Dubravica school, from the cinema, from the vet station to a variety of locations where trenches were dug. The court will also hear additional evidence from other civilians who were forced to dig trenches and we will present evidence in the course of this trial about the routine HVO practice of using civilians to dig trenches in various locations. Under the Defence proposal, Mr. President and your Honours, Dr Zeco's testimony about locations where these civilians were forced to dig trenches should be rejected, because he could not identify, four years later, the specific individuals who told him about those particular locations. The fact that Dr Zeco could not specifically name the individuals who told him that they were forced to dig trenches at these locations in the context and the circumstances of his captivity, in light of the other evidence adduced during the trial, suggests that the hearsay statement is reliable and should be considered by this Trial Chamber. What weight the Trial Chamber attaches to it is wholly within the judgement of the Trial Chamber and we respect your ability to make those determinations. Mr. President, I have nothing further to add on this particular point. Our brief is clear and our positions are articulated in it. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hayman, would you like to reply to that, without restating your arguments, just touching on the points raised by the Prosecution? If you care to do so, please proceed, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just for a moment. With respect to the evidence of Dr Zeco on this point, if one looks at what the good doctor related, and compares it to the testimony of the direct witnesses, witnesses who had direct knowledge of trench digging, we in fact will find, and the court will, if it is material in its deliberations, that Dr Zeco's information was in large part not reliable. He identified locations that have not been identified otherwise through direct witnesses, and indeed some of the locations he identified as being the sites of trench digging are on the wrong side of the front-line at the time. So if those anonymous hearsay declarations were truly material to this court's deliberations, and I think they will not be by the end of the case, if they were, we submit the court's reliance on those anonymous hearsay, out of court statements which we cannot possibly impeach or investigate those declarants because we do not know who they are, it would be error to rely on those for a material purpose in your deliberations. It is not a real issue, because I do not think those statements will be material, but consider another example. Just last week, Lieutenant Colonel Watters testified of the opinions of an interpreter who was present at a scene, the only evidence adduced, I submit to date in this case, that has any proffered connection to the accused's state of mind, and it is the out of court opinion statements of someone as to whom it has not even been shown is unavailable to testify, him or herself, in a legal sense. I think that is a shame, your Honour, that that evidence is in the record in this case under those circumstances. What I did not hear the Prosecutor address, and I think it is telling, is why should there not be a foundation for hearsay? Why should this court not know when hearsay evidence is being put in? Hearsay should not be slipped in and interwoven with other evidence, it should be there on the table for the court to see what it is and treat it in the way it deems appropriate. That is my response, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You have done, Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Fine, let me look towards fellow judges. Judge Riad, you have any questions or points you would like to make?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Hayman.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Just for my knowledge, you referred to Yugoslav law and I just wanted to know, do you have any more specific details about how they considered hearsay evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I do not, your Honour. I know that a witness is required to state his or her source, and that it is admitted and that it is generally viewed as suspect, but perhaps Mr. Nobilo, these sections are in his mother tongue, perhaps he can shed more light on that, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. According to the legal system I come from, hearsay evidence is accepted only exceptionally, if the court is unable to reach the source from whom the witness obtained the information, because if that person has relevant knowledge, then he is the suitable person to be called as a witness, rather than someone else who heard it from him. In the event that that is not possible, then the witness must indicate with precision who he heard it from, under which circumstances and all the other circumstances that may be of assistance in assessing the truthfulness of that evidence. That is the substance of the rules regarding hearsay evidence in the legal system I come from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nobilo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Judge Shahabuddeen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, I was very interested in your arguments. Do I understand you to be taking this position: you are not attacking the principle that hearsay evidence is admissible, you are directing your fire to the limits of admissibility of that type of evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Indeed, when I look at Rule 89(C) of the Rules of court, read with 89(A), I think there is a fair implication there favouring the view that hearsay is admissible. Then let us look at the Statute, Article 21(4)(e) to which you have correctly referred. On the footing that hearsay is in principle admissible, should the Tribunal construe the right of examination there as not necessarily equivalent to a right of confrontation with the source from which the hearsay evidence originally flows; would that be a correct view?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Well, I think to the extent Article 21 is based, it appears, on the European Human Rights Convention section, we know first of all that the European human rights court has interpreted that provision of the Convention to convey a right of confrontation and cross-examination, either in court or at some other time, and where it were the principal evidence upon which a criminal court relies is statements upon which the accused has not been able to exercise that right of confrontation, the convictions have been overturned, and we have cited those cases. I agree that under 21(4)(e) the term "witness" is used, which raises the question, who is the witness? If a witness comes into court and relates a conversation in which they obtained all their pertinent testimony from someone else, are they the witness, or are they a messenger? To give real meaning to 21(4)(e), should the court view the witness, the person really offering the proof, as the person who saw the event, made the statement which is been merely conveyed to the court. Our position is certainly that there has to be something more than simply a right to examine the witness who is present, because if all hearsay comes in and there is no other limitation, then every fact, every bit of testimony could be brought to this court by messengers, the accused would have no opportunity to actually confront and cross-examine the persons whose observations, opinions and so forth lay the foundation and form the structure for the Prosecutor's case, and that is not a role model for future successful international criminal jurisprudence, with all due respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I thank you. Let us look at this aspect. On the footing that hearsay is in principle admissible, is there an unlimited right of confrontation under Statute 21(4)(e) with the original source of the evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: It is not clear, your Honour, from the Statute or the Rules. I think the court would be prudent to adopt a balancing test, where a good number of observations, hearsay observations that do not form, if you will, the crux of the case, do not go to key elements, such as the only evidence admitted to date that might tend to bear on the accused's state of mind, those general observations, the court might well find as a result of a balance there is no violation of Article 21(4)(e); right, but as to others, I think there would be, so I agree, it is not an all or nothing venture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: So you would not take your thesis as far as to rely on Statute 21(4)(e) as designed entirely to ensure a right of confrontation?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I agree, I think you must read it in light of Rule 89.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Because if you did that, there would be difficulty reconciling a competence to admit hearsay evidence with an unlimited right of confrontation, would there not?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: There is, and that takes you to reliability and protecting the core rights of the accused to confront important evidence against him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: On that basis, that hearsay evidence is in principle admissible, would you have any observation on the proposition that what Statute 21(4)(e) is designed to give to a party, I think the Defence in this case, is a right to examine the witness in the box, and through him to attack the sources of any hearsay evidence which he produces, with a view to questioning the reliability of those sources, and to assisting the Tribunal to place a proper evaluation on those sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I think that would be a dangerous interpretation, and I think if that were the interpretation, then this court should have admitted the letter from President Izetbegovic, because Rule 21(4)(e) would not have excluded it. I think 21(4)(e) has to have something more than simply the right to examine the messenger in the case of hearsay and derivative evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Either there is an open-ended right of confrontation or, if that right is a limited one, then the right conferred by 21(4)(e) must be directed to examining the witness in the box and attacking his sources of information with a view to demonstrating to the court that the hearsay evidence which he has given is either not reliable or not probative. Is that a possible reading, do you think?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Your interpretation, your Honour, is a clear one. You take from the text a clear and strong interpretation, but I would respectfully submit that if the Prosecutor, if they brought in summary witnesses, if they brought in their investigators to recount the horrors and the tragedies we have heard of and did not bring in original witnesses, particularly with no showing of unavailability of those original source witnesses, the court would put its foot down under Rule 21(4)(e) and say, "no, it is inappropriate, you are treading on this man's basic rights under our Statute, under the European Human Rights Convention and under general principles in many national law systems".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Last question. What I have a slight difficulty with in your very interesting submissions is this: if you concede that hearsay evidence is admissible, is that wholly reconcilable with the view that the witness referred to in 21(4)(e) of the Statute includes the original source of the hearsay evidence and is not limited to the person testifying before the court?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I take your question as: if Rule 89 is a general rule of admissibility and admission, then how can 21(4)(e) reach anyone other than the witness in the box?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I think it has to, your Honour. If I am stretching the words, it is a time-honoured tradition in many, many courts and in jurisprudence in general that this court and this Tribunal has an obligation to protect the core rights of the accused, and if 21(4)(e) is limited to messengers in the witness box I think this court would not condone it and therefore I think there should be a rule that should recognise that the court has that power and that 21(4)(e) gives it that power, and that is what we are urging you to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, your arguments are very lucid and I appreciate them. My mind is completely open.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, dear colleagues. Your questions were quite relevant and I think you have cleared things up to me to a large extent. But first a question to the Prosecution. The testimony taken out of court, that testimony, is it given under oath or not? I have understood that it is not under oath, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, the statement that is made out of court is not under oath. The statement of the messenger, so to say, is under oath and is subject to

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: circumstances under which the statement was made and the reliability of the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I am talking about the witness who comes here, Dr Zeco for instance, when he made his statement, his initial statement to your investigators, he made that under oath, did he, is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: There is a declaration at the end of the witness statements, yes, Mr. President. I am not sure it is under oath, but there is a declaration attached to it and he has come and every witness who comes before this Chamber gives his or her testimony under oath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, fine. So we are talking about the prior statement. We would not really call it an oath, so the speaker, the witness, when he is in court, when he was speaking with the Office of the Prosecution three or four months earlier, was not under oath. I want to keep going if I might, Mr. Hayman, but if you have a point of clarification you would like to raise, go right ahead, Mr. Hayman.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I do not mean to interrupt counsel, but I can get the declaration. I am not completely cognisant --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: One second, you are interrupting Mr. Hayman who is interrupting me. Let us be clear here. We are quite open, but first let us hear the interruption of Mr. Hayman, then we will hear the interruption by Mr. Harmon and then I will come back to my question. Just a matter of clarification, Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Yes, it might save time. When I referred to statements not being under oath, I was referring to the statements of the declarants. So for example, these unidentified men in the Dubravica school who made statements to Dr Zeco, their statements were not under oath. As to prior statements of witnesses, I think there is a declaration, but there is no penalty to it. There is no exposure to any type of perjury or false statement charge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Fine. We can agree with that, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Fine, thank you. Now, Mr. Hayman, I have a question for you. When you plan your cross-examination, you have all the initial statements, that is on the basis of the order by the court, and you do refer to them, you cite them and you do confront the witness on the basis of their contents, so you do elaborate a plan when it comes to citing witnesses. There is nothing hindering you -- this is my question: what would stop you when it comes to a point you believe to be important, when it comes to the rights you have under Article 21(4)(e), why not have another witness come, or even the same witness cited, with reference to Dr Zeco, so that you could put questions to him on the reliability of what he heard. There is nothing hindering you from doing that, is there? Was that question clear to you, Mr. Hayman, or would you like me to spell it out a bit more? You are entitled to cross-examination, both let us take the example of Dr Zeco, Dr Zeco is there, so you can confront him and have him say that that is only hearsay evidence he is providing, and if you think that the testimony is so important, or the witness is so important in connection with the fact that it is hearsay and that it is prejudicial to your client, what would hinder you in three or four month's time, when you are calling your own witnesses, to either have him come back or call other witnesses that would show that his testimony was not appropriate? So as I said, this is in the context of Article 21(4)(e). You do have that right, do you not?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We have the ability to try and recall witnesses and bring in other witnesses. I think we have three basic objections to the practice that is being followed by the Prosecution now. One is there is no foundation being laid, so hearsay is being concealed, if you will, and I am not saying purposefully, but it is being concealed in the overall narrative of the witness, no attempt to sort it out and identify it is being made. That puts an unfair burden on the cross-examining party, because we all have limits to patience and this court is going to have a limit to this patience when it comes to recounting a narrative to try and sort out what is direct and derivative, so we think that is unfair. Second, where the declarants are anonymous, our ability to go out and investigate and bring in other witnesses who may be able to challenge those statements is very difficult, because an anonymous declarant with no time and place -- here we had a place, but we had a period of days; very, very difficult to do, I would submit, your Honour: Lastly, if something is truly critical -- I hope the court will not rely at all on the out of court opinions of this interpreter that were related by Lieutenant Colonel Watters, indeed for some of the reasons we were able to elicit on cross-examination, but with great difficulty, as the court will recall. There is a point at which basic rights are violated. We are simply asking the court, let us recognise that, so that we have a framework for future discussions in addressing these issues and these rights.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: But what about Rule 89? Are you saying that runs counter to the Statute? You are not going that far, are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Counter to the Statute. I think that, your Honour, one can look to Rule 89 to help understand and interpret Article 21, and as Judge Shahabuddeen has suggested and I agree with, Rule 89 strongly indicates that the right in Article 21(4)(e) is not absolute, it is not absolute. We agree with that, but I am not suggesting that Rule 89 is invalid, I am suggesting that this court should, indeed it must, give some teeth to Article 21(4)(e), because if the rule is, any and all hearsay comes in, there are no limits, then that is a very dangerous precedent. We should not allow that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: This may well be my last question, Mr. Hayman. Do you think the judges are able to make a distinction between direct testimony and hearsay testimony?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If it is not properly identified in the witness's testimony, no one can tell the difference, your Honour. We will recall perhaps the testimony --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I am a bit surprised, quite frankly, Mr. Hayman. All the legal systems throughout the world, I do not want to make specific reference to my own, you would be quite frightened away by my own. You should not plead in France, if you were before a French court, you would be quite unhappy there, but I think hearsay testimony is something you can find practically anywhere, it is a typical case. "Yes, I saw houses burning, I saw the houses burning in Ahmici", let us say, "I think they were set by the HVO", and then the question is, "why do you believe that?", "well, I heard someone say so"; it is hearsay. I think the judges can make a distinction between what the witness is saying and what the witness says he heard. Of course, I am not going to touch now on matters we will be raising in our deliberation, but we still have the status conference coming up, but maybe it is because we only rely on having witnesses present. Perhaps we could work on a different basis, where the Prosecution for now and the Defence later would be in the position to corroborate, where we would not be working just on the basis of testimony, but where we do have witnesses as the basis, of course, we do have this issue of direct and hearsay testimony. I maybe overdo it when it comes to reading texts, but I am very demanding and I think the texts say what they say for the time being. That, of course, does not hinder you, jurisprudence, playing its role in the judges' working on that basis and taking our decisions, but I am wondering, Mr. Hayman, whether you are not asking for the judges to adopt something from your legal system, which is not in the Statute and the Rules. The Statute and the Rules do not say, "do not do common law, do not do civil law", whatever. The judges are here to work on the basis of a number of rules and establish criminal responsibility. I think Judge Riad wanted to put a question on this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Chairman. I just want to sum up for myself. The real condition you are putting is some kind of procedural one, when you said there should be a method of implementation, when the witness should indicate what is hearsay and what is direct. That is really the very clear condition. The other conditions you mentioned were some kind of directives to the Tribunal when they consider their, let us say, reliability of the hearsay. When you said there should be a chain of declarants, a clear contest of the statement, these are almost directives for the judges, and not specific procedural conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I think that is right, your Honour, although where a witness knows the date and time and circumstance of the statement, we think that should be elicited, it should be a burden on the party putting the evidence forward, because that is a more efficient way to get that information on the table in front of your Honours and the parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: This would be a good thing to enlighten the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Absolutely, and it will save time, because you will not have the cross-examiners, which for the time being are myself and Mr. Nobilo, revisiting all these lengthy testimony to try and sort out, "what did you know and what did you not know?", because I am sure we have missed some. There are statements we have learned in the final questions of cross-examination that they were derivative and there are others I am sure we have missed and this Tribunal will never know if certain contents or certain items of evidence given were direct or hearsay, and that is not good. We think it should be put on the table so the court knows what evidence it has and that will lead to a more reliable fact-finding process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You have expressed clearly that there should be an indication of what is derivative and what is direct. That should be done in court. The other has to be done by the judges and you are advising them that they should take care of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I would submit that once a procedural rule is implemented, then the Tribunal will be in a position to implement whatever substantive rule on hearsay it finds appropriate, but without a procedural rule to identify hearsay, then there can be no meaningful test for reliability, there can be no meaningful test to afford whatever Article 21 rights there are that are implicated here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: One last question, Mr. Hayman. Your arguments are so engaging that I am tempted to put one last question to you. If you accept that hearsay evidence is in principle admissible, then would you think it right to leave it to the judges to apply a customary rule of evaluation which would take into account, for example, whether the particular hearsay evidence is firsthand hearsay, or second hand hearsay, or third hand hearsay; you know judges would normally take account of that aspect. Would you think the judges might be left to take that into account?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If the hearsay has been identified as such, and the circumstances are on the table, I think the court is free to evaluate reliability as it sees fit and if there is sufficient reliability, hearsay should be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Let us go back to your remark about if the circumstances are before the court; would it not be open to counsel for a party to help to place those circumstances before the court by examining the witness who is actually in front of the court on points relevant to the determination as to whether the particular hearsay evidence is firsthand hearsay or second hand hearsay or third hand hearsay et cetera, and would that not help the court?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: It would, and that is part of counsel's obligation, although we think a foundation should be laid first, so that it is identified. Then we can pull it out and your Honours can conduct whatever evaluation is appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, if you might allow me a comment. You said that the counsel for the accused is not in the position, does not have the time, the means to make these distinctions, and you say that the judges should come up with a rule. Judges coming up with a rule -- judges apply rules, they do not go about creating them. For instance, would you go so far as to think that the judges should be playing a more active role at trial, because you have to be consistent? You yourself who have the initial statements, if you cite them in your cross-examination, it is hard for you to distinguish the direct from the derivative evidence, it is even more difficult for the judges. What they can do in the event of doubt, they can exclude following evidence, cross-examination, to the effect that the houses had all been burned and that that was not relevant evidence. Do you think that we should be playing a more active role, we should have a full case file and that we should have a plan for questioning? I am already moving into the ground of the status conference, as it were. I take it you will say no. That is what I would assume.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: No, your Honour, we want the court, we want your Honours to be more involved in the active trial of the case, because we think that will speed the process. But as to hearsay, what I am saying, your Honour, is, it is counsel's job to develop the circumstances of hearsay evidence so that the court -- with the court so it can be evaluated, but where it is not identified and no attempt is made, and no attempt is being made in the Prosecutor's presentations, to identify what is hearsay and what is not, that quite frankly is just not a sound procedure. Certainly the court can direct matters like foundation and other procedural matters that are totally within the court's discretion, we believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Fine. Well, we are running a little later than planned. I think we can leave it at that, if there are not any other points of clarification in relation to hearsay. Then I am going to give you the floor, Mr. Hayman. It is calling into question the decision of the judges, as it were, because we have taken a decision, and you want that decision to be reconsidered by the very same judges, so I am a bit concerned. Maybe you could tell us a little bit more about your motion that dates back to September as well, so this Chamber is to reconsider the decision that had to do with exculpatory evidence which had been regarded as authentic, so could you briefly sum up your main argument, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, thank you. We thought long and hard before we brought this motion, your Honours, because it is delicate, indeed in some ways uncomfortable to ask the Trial Chamber to reconsider a decision that has been made, and I do not think we have done it very often, but we have done it here, because we think this is very important. By this motion, we ask the Chamber to reconsider the ruling that even after a document -- that ruling holds that even after a document has been authenticated, Defence counsel must provide the Prosecution -- the court has said the court, but also importantly provide to the Prosecution -- information concerning how we obtained the particular copy of the document that was placed before the witness and authenticated, thereby disclosing our sources and methods of investigation. We believe, your Honours, and if one looks to how this issue arose, this was not raised by the Prosecutor with respect to any true concern about the authenticity of the document and documents that had been put in front of the witness, Mr. Djidic, and that had been identified. It was an attempt by the Prosecutor to gain a tactical advantage by imposing a discovery obligation on the Defence that does not exist in the Statute of the Rules, and that is unprecedented in any other Trial Chamber or any other proceeding before this Tribunal. No other Tribunal -- no other Trial Chamber in any other case, our search of the records indicates, has imposed any type of requirement of this nature. Indeed, the court has alluded to a new motion, which we will respond to next week, in which the Prosecutor seeks to make another discovery obligation and impose it on the Defence. We think that is telling as well. In our reply brief, your Honours, we discussed the differences between authenticity, authorship, source --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Which motion are you referring to, Mr. Hayman? Just to be perfectly clear. You said that in your reply --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: In the response to this motion regarding the authentication of documents, your Honour. I hope that has gotten before the court. I know it has been translated and I have seen our reply brief in both languages of the Tribunal. So we attempted to clarify those terms, I will not repeat. Importantly, we do not by our motion seek to restrain the Prosecutor or restrain the court from questioning the authenticity of documents put before it. Absolutely not. The Prosecutor is free to express every concern about the authenticity of documents; so is the court. But please, if one looks at their response, there has been no concern stated about the authenticity of the documents in question. They have yet to articulate any concern about authenticity; indeed if you ask, "how were these documents authenticated?", they were authenticated by a Prosecution witness. Are they attacking their own witness? They are seeking to gain a tactical advantage by creating a discovery obligation and imposing it on the Defence which does not exist and should not, even more importantly, should not exist. The issue is, how is authenticity to be determined in proceedings before the Tribunal. We submit authenticity is to be determined through the testimony of competent witnesses or by stipulation between the parties. Indeed, if a party wishes to contest authenticity after a witness has authenticated a document, it can ask that the document be held in abeyance and that the party either conduct voir dire of the witness, or that the document be held in abeyance until cross-examination on the document has been concluded. That did not happen here. There were no such requests. There was simply a request for Defence counsel to assume the role of witnesses and disclose what we believe is confidential and privileged information regarding our sources and methods of investigation. But whatever Mr. Nobilo and I are, we are advocates. We are not witnesses. It would be very different if we had been summoned in a civil law system to come and give evidence to the court. Given the adversary nature, the fundamental adversary nature of the proceedings in this Tribunal, we submit it is wrong to impose on counsel, against counsel's will and without the consent of counsel's client, that is counsel for the accused, to compel us to reveal this information concerning our confidential sources and methods. To do that, we submit, confuses the proper role of counsel in what is fundamentally an adversary system here in the International Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia. A subsidiary point is: how do we handle documents that have not yet been authenticated? There have been some conflicting opinions voiced in the course of the proceedings on this point. Indeed, it has been suggested by the Prosecution's office that if a document has not yet been authenticated, it cannot be shown to a witness. A witness cannot be questioned about the document. We do not agree with that. First, we have to be free to show a document to a witness in order to authenticate it, or to try; and second, there will be occasions when a document that a particular witness cannot authenticate and a document that has not been authenticated by any prior witness needs to be shown to the witness in the box and questioned about the document, because if we are not able to do that, and the document is subsequently authenticated and admitted, we may have to recall all the prior witnesses who had relevant testimony to give about that document. So what I am suggesting is: documents that cannot be authenticated yet, they should be marked for identification, and we should be free to show them, and the Prosecution as well, when we come to the Defence case, to show them to witnesses in the box, again with due regard for the efficiency and speed of the proceedings, and question those witnesses about them prior to admission. Of course, if the document is never authenticated and admitted, then it will never be evidence, and we do not contest that. Lastly, there is a subsidiary issue here with respect to the Rule 68 information, and those are documents such as Mil Info Summs that the Prosecution has given us pursuant to its obligation under Rule 68 to provide exculpatory information. There, we have run into a problem that these documents are so heavily redacted, many of them, that it is not clear exactly what the document is. It may have a hand-written notation at the top "Mil Info Summ" and a date, but it is not clear, for example, as Lieutenant Colonel Watters pointed out, is a particular item of information in a Mil Info Summ, where is it from, what is it, what is the information? Indeed, is it a Mil Info Summ? We have offered some of those documents early on; more recently this objection has not been made, perhaps because we filed our motion, but early on, an objection was made that the Prosecutor did not know how it came upon these documents that it had given to us and therefore the document could not be admitted, because the Defence only knew we got it from the Prosecution and the Prosecution could not say from the records available here in court where it got it. We do think this is an untenable position by the Prosecutor and all we ask on that subsidiary issue, which is fully raised in the briefs, is that the court address it, give us a clear ruling, so that either the Prosecutor is obliged to tell us the nature of these documents, the date and so forth, or if not, the court state that that request is denied. Thank you, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, please? First, I would like to ask Mr. Dubuisson before we hear Mr. Kehoe; I have got the reply from the Prosecutor, is there another document, just to be clear on this? Mr. Hayman, just a clarification to be perfectly clear. I had the feeling that there were some arguments you just put forward that were not in your initial motion. Have you broadened the scope of your argumentation? Should that be the case, was that your right of reply that you have used, as it were? Maybe I could ask the Registrar whether we have had another motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I think my comments, your Honour, were within the scope of our initial motion. We did file a reply brief on 21st November, and it has been translated into both languages of the Tribunal, and I have a copy of the French.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, but there is no accusation here, just I had not had it. With regard to the brief comments you just made, I had the feeling you had included several ingredients when it came to the conclusions in your motion. They were focused mainly on the source in connection with the decisions relating to the obligations which we thought applied to both the Prosecution and the Defence, so with regard to the source and the authors of some documents. That is why I put that question to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it may be there is a greater semantic issue here than I have given treatment to, and that is, we believe whether a document is authentic, who is the author, and what is the source of a particular document brought to court, those are very different things. We do not seek to limit anyone's ability, the Prosecutor or the court's, to scrutinise the authenticity of any document presented in court. The source of a document is also different from the author, we believe, and the issue raised by the Prosecutor was not the authorship of a document, the issue was source; how did the Defence obtain, physically obtain the copy of an otherwise authentic document which the Prosecutor's own witnesses had authenticated, and that simply involves, how did we get it? Did we buy it on the black market? Did we get it from the Prosecution's witness? Was it mailed to us anonymously? Whatever, how did we get it, how did we physically come to have it. With all due respect, the gist of our motion is -- I am sorry, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: That is not really the motion that was initially filed in connection with our decision. You are addressing now the issue of how you can obtain certain documents. I do not think that in the decisions we took we in any way set limits to the obtaining of documents. In any event, there are two other decisions in particular when it came to the production of documentary evidence; but as I have not read your latest motion, maybe that is the problem I am having.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I did re-read our motion last night, and again, there may be an issue of semantics, and I do not know how "source" is being translated, I do not know how "authenticity" is being translated, but our position, I think, we have sought to make it very clear and very consistent from the outset and that is, our methods of investigation are private and confidential. If a document is authenticated and the Prosecutor should have the opportunity to contest that, ask competent witnesses, express its concerns to the court. Those are two separate issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Okay, fine. Mr. Kehoe, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President and your Honours, good morning. The motion on behalf of the Defence is essentially a motion to revisit an issue that this court has decided, i.e. requesting both the Prosecution and the Defence to give sources for their information. What the Defence motion is tantamount to requesting is a restriction of the powers of this Trial Chamber, quite clearly set forth in 89(e). This Trial Chamber, as any Trial Chamber, has the right and the power to request verification of the authenticity of a document, verification. Why? Why, so this court can make a proper decision concerning the accuracy of that document, whether that document is complete, whether that document should be given a great amount of weight or whether that document should be given a lesser amount of weight. The powers set forth in Rule 89(e) are, of course, supplemented by the powers given to the court for the ordering of a trial as promulgated in Rule 98, which by its very nature is extremely broad and permits this court, the President and the Trial Chamber, to request additional witnesses and call witnesses and ask for additional evidence as the court sees fit. Suffice it to say -- and I have no intention, your Honours, of revisiting every argument that we made in our papers -- suffice it to say that no power given to this court should be restricted in any fashion. Asking questions concerning the reliability of the document, asking questions concerning the source of that document, asking any question that this Trial Chamber sees fit in order to make a decision. As 89(e) sets forth and as interpreted by the Tadic court, the reliability of the document goes to the probative nature of the document and that particular issue all too often is tied up in where this document came from. We saw a telling example of that particular instance in this court, approximately a week and a half ago. Unfortunately, several weeks after we filed the motion or response to counsel's motion. Where did we see that? We saw that in the BBC tape that was presented by the Defence, where the tape, as it was presented, first in the cross-examination of Captain Tudor Ellis and then in the cross-examination of Lieutenant Colonel Bryan Watters, showed the editing of a piece of tape that had been provided to counsel, a tape that came from the British Broadcasting Corporation, which would make it appear that British battalion soldiers were arming Muslim soldiers. On further reflection, when one looks at a little bit more of that tape from the BBC, it quite clearly appears, and is, an officer in an UN vehicle examining a weapon. The court needs to have the power and the right to examine where a document comes from at every source. The Prosecutor goes so far as to say that even if the Defence and the Prosecution exists on the omission of a document or a tape or a piece of evidence, this court still has the power, should it decide to do so, to ask the parties for additional information concerning the source of that information. That is clearly delineated under 89(e) and more broadly set forth, as I noted previously, under Rule 98. This limits no person or party in this courtroom. Counsel has argued to you just several minutes ago that he is unable to use the particular documents that he wants in cross-examination because it has not been sourced. I beg to differ with counsel and I will rely on the record and your Honours' memories, but the only restriction that has been put on Defence counsel and the Defence in the use of any documents has been their ultimate admissibility. The documents themselves have been used extensively in cross-examination of Prosecution witnesses to date. The only ruling that has come from the court, Mr. President, is a holding of these particular documents and these particular pieces of evidence in abeyance, until a source has been provided to the court. But if I may reiterate just once again, there has been no restriction by this Trial Chamber on the Defence in using unsourced documents in the cross-examination of witnesses. So the question is: given how this court has enabled the Defence to use these documents extensively, and has merely requested additional information that the court desires concerning the source, it is quite clear, as we sit some months into trial, there has been absolutely no prejudice to the Defence whatsoever in their ability to develop their information as they see fit and to develop their defence. The reality of the situation, your Honours, is it just simply has not happened. This court has given generous free rein to the Defence to use those documents. There is an argument in Defence counsel's motions concerning the chilling effect on using or being forced to divulge the source of some of this documentation. Again, I will not address this extensively, but suffice it to say, your Honours and Mr. President, that this court has been very open to the use and the development of protective measures to ensure that anybody providing information, that person's physical being would be safeguarded. There are more than ample Rules set forth and Articles set forth in the Tribunal's Statute and Rules to give any protection to the source of information that that particular source needs, so any argument that somehow, in some way, given this circumstance in this courtroom that the inability to use those documents chills the Defence, I submit to your Honours is without foundation, given the practice and procedure to date in this Trial Chamber. It just simply does not exist. Lastly, concerning the documents that Defence counsel says have been unsourced by the Prosecution. There has been, let me say, on several points, due to a request by the Defence, and I know your Honours know this, there has not been reciprocal discovery because it was the decision of the Defence to choose not to operate that way. Nevertheless, literally thousands of documents have been supplied to the Defence under Rule 66(A), as is the Prosecutor's obligation to provide counsel with the confirming material that was given to the confirming judge and also under Rule 68, which is exculpatory information. Thousands of pages, thousands. In previous arguments before this court, we have told this court, and again I reiterate, that, pursuant to the court's instructions, the Office of the Prosecutor reviewed hundreds and thousands of pages of documents to comply with our Rule 68 obligations. The only request that we make concerning that information is a simple one. If the Defence asks the Office of the Prosecutor for the source of a particular document that has been provided to the Defence, either pursuant to Rule 66(A) or pursuant to Rule 68, they only need ask where it came from, but to force the Prosecutor to go through an hourless, extensive process, the resources for which we do not have. To source every document, most of which will not be used by the Defence and have not been used to date, is a burden that we simply cannot undertake, given the significant manpower shortages that beleaguer the Office of the Prosecutor. Your Honours, I offer, my colleagues and I offer the solution, an extremely reasonable solution, that counsel, notwithstanding our lack of reciprocal discovery, simply ask us, "what is the source of this document?", and we will tell them. As I said at the outset, Mr. President, your Honours, I have no intention to reiterate and go through chapter and verse all of our arguments, I think our arguments are adequately set forth and one thing about lawyers is from time to time they stand up and speak too much, so at that point, Mr. President, your Honours, I have concluded my argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Well, that is a bit of self-censorship there, Mr. Kehoe. I do not know whether Mr. Hayman has any points related to this he wants to touch on very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Perhaps I am not as wise as my learned friend and colleague. If I could just have a couple of minutes, your Honour? Rule 89(F). It is a very interesting rule, "verification of authenticity". What does that mean? If authenticity is established, what does it mean to verify authenticity? To have two different independent sources establishing authenticity, is that the requirement? We submit once authenticity is established to the court's satisfaction then as long as it is relevant, there it is, it should be admitted. Verification of authenticity cannot mean that after a party has authenticated a document and the court is satisfied that it is authentic, that then there is some other inquiry to be performed. There simply is not. We do not question, as I said, the court's authority and power to ensure that only authentic documents are treated as such by this court. That is only appropriate. The issue of the BBC tape is a red herring. First of all, the Defence was very clear when we presented that tape that we did not know if the witness could authenticate it; first Captain Ellis and then Lieutenant Colonel Watters. They were not, and it was not authenticated. It has not been admitted. Indeed, the adversary system, where competent witnesses testify about context, authenticity and so forth, it did the function that it should do and we now know that this piece of tape, in a medley of tapes, was taken from a BBC tape, because Lieutenant Colonel Watters was able to tell us that. We also now know from the testimony of Tudor Ellis that ITN created a medley tape with many many little bits of pieces, stuck together with rock music, if you will, and other audio components, a tape we are still trying to get so we can see how it was edited and what else was on it. So the process worked with respect to the tape, and the issue is a red herring, we think. I am pleased that Mr. Kehoe concedes that a document, even if not authenticated, may be marked and a witness can be questioned about it, so I think the court can take it that the parties agree on that. But we do not agree that that means there is no prejudice to the Defence from having a per se rule of excluding authentic Defence documents, unless Defence counsel takes the stand and testifies as to our methods of obtaining those documents. The fact is, we need to know what the rule is going to be, so that we can carry out our investigation appropriately, and we are being constrained, there is a chilling effect on our ability to do that and indeed, if this ruling is not altered, we may well have to make file under seal for the appellate court, should there ever be an appellate proceeding, an offer of proof as to how our investigation has been constrained, what sources have refused to provide additional documents related to this court's ruling, so that the record is clear in that regard. Lastly, the Prosecutor asks that to deal with the issue of documents the Prosecutor has given us that we give them notice before our cross-examinations of what documents we will use so that they can tell us the source. That would not further the integrity of the fact-finding process before this court, because we should not be telling witnesses before their cross-examination what they are going to be shown on cross-examination so that they can artificially prepare to deal with those issues. It is simply not wise, it is an attempt to create a new and yet another discovery obligation and impose it on us, the Defence, and I note that if the court modifies its prior ruling so that the emphasis is on authenticity, not how the Defence obtained a document, then there is no need for this second issue to be addressed at all, because it will not be a barrier to the court's consideration of documents that originated with the Prosecution, were given to us and that we are tendering to witnesses and then seeking admission. Thank you, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Fine. Fellow judges, any questions, comments?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, just a question to understand the bottom line which you are suggesting. You require from the Prosecutor to authenticate any document, is that right, if necessary?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, as to documents they gave us under the discovery rules, if there is a requirement imposed by the court, a per se rule, that unless the court knows how a party obtained a document it shall not be admitted, then we cannot admit those documents. Unless the Prosecutor articulates how they obtained it, we are totally dependent on them. If that is to be the rule, then we are asking the court to order the Prosecutor to tell us how they came by these different documents, what are they, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But you refuse reciprocity. You refuse to be treated the same way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
