utterances.text: No, we do not think any counsel, Prosecution or Defence, should have to become witnesses and, in effect, give testimony about their methods and sources of investigation. We think documents that come before the Tribunal should be treated in a standard bilateral and reciprocal way. The inquiry is: is it authentic? If the court is satisfied it is authentic, then it should be admitted, if it is otherwise relevant; if it is not satisfied, it should be excluded, but it should be excluded because the court questions the authenticity of the document, therefore it is not probative if it is not authentic, not based on some per se rule relating to the parties' methods of investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, I was interested in your last remark, which I understood this way, that your request that the Prosecution in making available to you any exculpatory statements should also provide information as to authenticity, and I thought what you were saying now was that that request is only maintained if the court maintains its original ruling.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I think there is a link. There are some independent reasons why they should have to do it, but those reasons are compounded if the court has a per se "source" rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I ask that because I see in your reply at page 6, at the bottom, that you are saying there: "Although the Defence urges the Trial Chamber to reconsider its ruling, whether it does so or not, the Prosecution should be required to provide the Defence with information, if known to the Prosecutor, regarding the author, origin, date, et cetera." There is no link there, is there?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, as I said, there are independent reasons they should do it, because some of the documents we have gotten are so heavily redacted, it is hard to tell what they are. So I think there are independent reasons, but if there is no per se source rule, then that rule is eliminated as a reason and quite frankly that rule is the problem that has brought this issue to, for us, a crisis proportion, to crisis level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you. May I turn now to the Prosecution. Mr. Prosecutor, a court is jealous of its powers, so when you say that Mr. Hayman is effectively asking the Tribunal to impose restrictions on its powers, you are striking a chord to which a court might be expected to be very responsive. Would you subscribe to the view that Mr. Hayman does not need to be apologetic about asking the court to review its earlier decision?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Judge Shahabuddeen, Mr. Hayman does not have to be apologetic about asking the court to review a prior decision. My point at the outset, Judge Shahabuddeen, was casting this argument in its most direct light, and that is a request to limit the court's powers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I put this to you, I take it you accept the customary dichotomy which distinguishes between admissibility and weight.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I do, judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Am I right in understanding Mr. Hayman to be taking this position: if there is a witness in the box who says, "I recognise this document, I know the signature, I have even seen it before", that the document there upon becomes admissible, and any other inquiries concerning authenticity or source or whatever will then go only to weight. That is how I understand him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Judge, there could very well be situations where that is the case and there could very well be situations where neither party has any objection to admissibility of a document on that level. Nevertheless, it is still the power of a Trial Chamber to request where this document came from. Let us turn, if you will, to the particular tape, and hypothetically speaking, let us say that Captain Ellis, when he was testifying, said, "yes, I do recall a tape like that", and given the playing of that tape on the BBC, one might say, "I remember seeing something like that on television". As we move down the line, this tape is shown as coming from the BBC. Even if that initial Defence tape came into evidence, this court could still question its source. The position of the Prosecutor, judge, is that no power concerning any document, any piece of evidence, no power to question that document -- no restrictions on the power to question that document should be imposed on this Trial Chamber, no power.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I understand you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If at the final hour the court says, "notwithstanding a lack of source, given the fact that a particular witness has authenticated it, we are going to admit it into evidence"; that, of course, is up to the Trial Chamber, it is within the discretion of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I see. So the Trial Chamber could do that. Then let us look at Rule 89(e), to which both sides referred. Would I be right in saying that a possible interpretation of that rule is that it gives the court a power to request verification of authenticity, but that the exercise of that power in a particular case is not meant to impose a condition precedent on the admissibility of the evidence in question; whether the evidence is admissible depends on whether it is relevant and whether it is probative, and it may be all of those things even in the absence of verification of authenticity. How do you react to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Judge, that could very well be the case, and if at that juncture, as we come to the end of the trial, the court is satisfied concerning those conditions, i.e. authenticity, and believes that the document has been verified, then the Office of the Prosecutor would have no objection to the court admitting that document into evidence, again, within the discretion of the Trial Chamber, to make that decision as the Trial Chamber sees fit. I do not intend to argue in any way, shape or form on any restriction to that accord. To the contrary, the court has asked, due to a multitude of factors, dealing with xerox copies, dealing with edited tapes, that the source of these documents be presented to the Trial Chamber. If the Trial Chamber requests that, the Office of the Prosecutor will comply and so should the Defence. Again, however, at the end of the day, if the court believes that a document has been authenticated, the court believes it should be admitted, then so be it, it should be admitted on that score.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Good. So I understand you then to be taking the position that Rule 89(e), which confers on the court a power to request verification of authenticity, goes not to admissibility but to weight. The court could well be in a position where, its request for verification not having been complied with, it proceeds to attach little or no weight to the particular document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I can answer that by being just a degree more expansive, judge, I think that it goes to both. The court can, because of lack of verification, exclude the document, as is permitted by Rule 89, or admit it and then gauge its weight accordingly, so I think that the Rule as it is written provides the Chamber with a full spectrum of possibilities: admissibility; not admissibility; if admissibility, the weight to be given to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You say Rule 89(e) can also go to admissibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, judge, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: That is a view that will need to be considered. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Just a question for Mr. Hayman. Authenticity of a document, how would you define that? Is it linked to the source?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Authenticity, your Honour, is the question of whether the document is what it purports to be. If a document is an agreement between two warring factions, dated on a certain date and has signatures on it, is it in fact the document that was created on or before that date and signed and executed on that date and is it a true copy, if not the original. That is how I would define authenticity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: But when you talk about true copy, already there we are in the area of source.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I think not, your Honour, with the great respect I have for you and the court, because with respect to a document, a witness can look at the document such as Mr. Djidic did, and said, "yes, this is the document, I have seen it before, I recognise the names, I recognise the signature, this is the document that we generated on or about this date", and that is what is different about documents from physical evidence, as I note in my reply brief. You have to have a chain of custody for a blood sample or a fingerprint or a human hair, because they can change, they can not only be altered but they can deteriorate and change over time, depending on conditions of storage. But a document, if you are talking about the contents of a document and not a fingerprint on it, no court requires a chain of custody for documents, I submit. What is required is that a witness authenticate it, it is what it purports to be and if not the original, it is a true copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: But could you conceive of situations where all the parties authenticate a document and where the document turns out at the end of the day not to have been authentic and if one had knowledge of the source, one would have known it. Let me give an example of a notary act. This is in France, I assume the same goes for the Netherlands and the United States. You have something equivalent when there is a transfer of property. It is the source that is being authenticated, as it were, so if you turn it round, the day you have a public notary's document, you know the source and you know that it is authentic. I am not challenging the distinctions that can be made under 89(e), the customary distinction between the probative value and identification and authentication remains valid, but I think you would agree with me that it is a bit more subtle than that. With the videotape, that in this connection, I will not tell you what my views on this matter are, but that does go to show that in certain cases there can be some confusion; everyone can agree that this is a given videotape, everyone can agree that it is from a given television programme, but that notwithstanding, when it comes to authenticity, no problem there, probative value will agree here, everyone will draw their own conclusions as far as probative value goes, but I do think there is a highly complex link between superficial identification and authenticity, and authenticity is already a step in respect of probative value. In your system, perhaps, you are saying if everybody agrees that a document is authentic, it is going to have a particular value. I do not think that is always the case. But these are just comments I am making, that is not meant as a question, unless there is something you would like to add, Mr. Hayman.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: To compliment the court, I think those are good comments. I think to have a certified copy of a document that exists in a court house or a property record office, or the county clerk's office, that is always desirable, but in this case, we are going to find that in the chaos of war there are no central repositories, central archives with complete, certainly not with complete sets of documents. In the chaos of war, people took documents, people fled, and so the type of certified copies, with a notary stamp or whatever on them, are going to be very hard to come by in this case, and it is very important that the documents presented not be limited to a category which in many cases will be unattainable by either party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hayman. I just wanted to make that comment to show that the matter was perhaps a bit more complex and subtle. I think we have done for the time being, we are going to resume in about 15 minutes or so for about 45 minutes, an hour, take stock without re-examination. It is the usual status conference then in connection with the trial of General Blaskic. So the court stands adjourned, we are going to be having a closed session, a status conference, in about 15 minutes time. (11.40 am)
